company_name: Qfin Holdings, Inc. (formerly Qifu Technology, Inc.; formerly 360 DigiTech)
overview: Qfin Holdings operates Qifu Technology, an AI-empowered credit-tech platform in China (primary consumer app: Qifu Jietiao / formerly 360 Jietiao) that connects underbanked consumers and small businesses with licensed financial institution funding partners. Rather than lending directly from its own balance sheet in most cases, the company provides borrower acquisition, credit assessment, risk management, and post-facilitation/collection technology services, earning fees from financial institutions and, to a declining extent, taking credit risk on a portion of facilitated loans. As of year-end 2024 it had cumulatively facilitated roughly RMB2.2 trillion in loans to over 34 million borrowers through partnerships with over 165 financial institutions, making it one of the largest independent loan-facilitation platforms listed in the US, alongside peers LexinFintech, FinVolution and Lufax.

business_model.summary: Qfin earns fees for operating the technology and risk layer between borrowers and licensed lenders (banks, trust companies, consumer finance companies). Historically the business ran a hybrid 'capital-light' (pure fee-based, off-balance-sheet risk) and 'capital-heavy' (on-balance-sheet/guarantee, taking credit risk via trusts and its own licensed entities) model; management has been shifting the mix toward capital-light to reduce balance-sheet risk and regulatory exposure, though a tightening funding market in 2026 has disrupted this transition. Revenue is transactional/volume-based (tied to loan facilitation and origination volume) rather than subscription-style recurring revenue, making it sensitive to loan volume, take rates, and credit losses in any given quarter.

revenue_streams.name: Credit-driven services (capital-heavy, on-balance-sheet risk via trusts/licensed lending entities)
Platform services (capital-light loan facilitation, referral and post-origination fees)
revenue_streams.trend: declining in 2026 amid regulatory/funding stress, prior years growing

revenue_streams.name: Other (technology licensing, ADS program fees, other)

business_model.customer_type: Two-sided: (1) individual consumers and small/micro business owners in China seeking unsecured installment credit, largely underserved by traditional banks; (2) B2B — over 165 financial institution funding partners (banks, trust companies, consumer finance companies) that are the company's actual customers for its risk-management and facilitation technology
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Mainland China operations; ADSs traded on Nasdaq (QFIN) and Class A ordinary shares dual-listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (3660.HK) since 2023

competitive_position.market_position: One of the four leading independent (non-Big-Tech-platform) credit-tech/loan-facilitation companies in China, alongside LexinFintech, FinVolution and Lufax; a tier below Ant Group, Tencent/WeBank and JD.com, which have superordinate scale, cheaper funding, and in-house super-app distribution. Qfin differentiates on AI-driven underwriting/risk models and a long operating history (legacy 360 Finance relationship with Qihoo 360).

moat_factors.description: Years of loan performance data (34M+ borrowers, RMB2.2tn+ cumulative volume) feed underwriting models that have delivered industry-leading delinquency metrics (e.g., improving C-M2 and 30-day collection rates in 2026 even as volumes fell), a genuine technical edge versus smaller platforms

165+ bank/trust/consumer-finance partnerships create switching costs and distribution scale that smaller platforms lack, though these relationships are now a point of fragility as funding partners pull back industry-wide
Large installed base (268M+ registered users) and historical Qihoo 360 brand affiliation support lower customer acquisition costs versus new entrants

Holds licensed lending entities (small loan companies, etc.) that provide some barrier to unlicensed competitors, but regulatory barriers currently cut against incumbents as rules tighten across the whole sector

weaknesses: No true network effect or recurring/subscription revenue — the model is transactional and highly exposed to loan volume and credit cycle swings
Minimal pricing power: a hard regulatory price cap (annualized APR capped around 24%) compresses take rates across the entire industry, Qfin included
Heavy dependence on third-party funding partners whose willingness to fund loans can evaporate quickly in a liquidity-stressed market (seen acutely in mid-2026)
Commoditized underwriting technology — AI/risk-model edges are difficult to defend long-term as competitors invest similarly
Geographic concentration: 100% China revenue with no diversification outside a single, heavily regulated domestic market

growth_drivers: Secular underbanked-consumer credit demand in China — large population still underserved by traditional bank lending
Shift toward a 'capital-light' fee-based model that reduces balance-sheet risk and regulatory capital needs (strategic priority, though disrupted in 2026)
AI-driven underwriting improvements (declining delinquency/C-M2 ratios, improving collection rates) that could support margin recovery once volumes stabilize

International/overseas expansion exploration by some peers (e.g., Southeast Asia) as a hedge against China-only concentration — a potential future lever for Qfin, though not yet a material contributor

Consolidation of the loan-facilitation sector: weaker/smaller platforms are being squeezed out by tightening rules, potentially leaving survivors like Qfin with a larger share of a smaller, more disciplined market
Capital return to shareholders (dividends, historically buybacks) if cash generation stabilizes post-shakeout

business.description: Total loan facilitation/origination volume fell roughly 2.5% sequentially in Q2 2026 and management guided to a further meaningful decline in Q3 2026 as risk controls tighten amid funding stress

A liquidity crisis at peer platform Juzi Digitech in June 2026 triggered a broad tightening of funding availability from banks/trusts across the whole loan-facilitation sector, directly constraining Qfin's ability to originate loans
Revenue depends on a relatively small number of large financial institution funding partners; loss of a major partner could materially impair origination capacity
Capital-heavy (on-balance-sheet) portion of the business bears direct credit losses from borrower defaults in a weakening Chinese consumer environment

financial.description: Non-GAAP net income fell from RMB1.85bn (Q2 2025) to RMB454.9m (Q2 2026), and management guided Q3 2026 non-GAAP net income down 67-73% YoY — an extreme swing for a company previously seen as a stable cash generator
All revenue and earnings are RMB-denominated while ADS dividends and valuation are USD-referenced, creating FX translation risk for US investors
BofA cited the absence of share buybacks as removing a key valuation support in 2026; dividend payout ratio (~30% in H1 2026) is being maintained but off a much lower earnings base

regulatory.description: Chinese regulators have capped all-in annualized loan costs at roughly 24%, compressing platform take rates and borrower eligibility sector-wide

New rules effective 2026 from the PBOC and seven other ministries restrict online marketing of loans/insurance/deposits by loan-assisting platforms, directly targeting the customer-acquisition channel Qfin and peers rely on

A joint Ministry of Public Security/National Financial Regulatory Administration campaign launched April 2026 targets illegal financial intermediaries and loan brokers, adding compliance costs and uncertainty across the sector

Regulators have tightened oversight of bank partnerships with online lending platforms and restricted platform access to credit reporting and payment infrastructure, structurally narrowing the addressable funding pool

Qfin's China-based auditor is not currently PCAOB-inspected; under the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act, ADSs face potential forced delisting from Nasdaq if audit inspection access is not maintained, though the Hong Kong dual listing (3660.HK) provides a fungible alternative venue that mitigates (but does not eliminate) the practical impact on US investors

regulatory.risk: VIE structure / Chinese government intervention risk
regulatory.description: Operations run partly through variable-interest-entity and licensed-lending-entity structures subject to Chinese government discretion; broader US-China tensions over data security and capital markets add tail risk

macro.description: Weak domestic consumption and a soft labor/property market reduce both loan demand and repayment capacity among Qfin's target underbanked borrower base
The Juzi Digitech liquidity crisis demonstrated that stress at one platform can rapidly spread to funding availability for the whole loan-facilitation industry
Broader tensions (tariffs, capital markets restrictions, scrutiny of Chinese ADRs) create headline and policy risk independent of company fundamentals

macro_factors.industry_outlook: China's online/consumer loan-facilitation industry is in the midst of a regulator-driven shakeout: rate caps (~24% APR), new restrictions on online marketing of loan products, tighter bank-partnership and data-access rules, and a public-security-led crackdown on illegal lending intermediaries are compressing volumes and margins across all independent platforms. Deutsche Bank expects loan-book contraction to extend into Q4 2026. The survivors (Qfin, LexinFintech, FinVolution, Lufax) may eventually consolidate share from exiting smaller/weaker players, but near-term the entire sector is shrinking.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — loan volume, credit losses and fee income are all directly tied to the Chinese consumer credit cycle and to episodic liquidity events at peer platforms (e.g., Juzi Digitech) that can trigger sector-wide funding pullbacks
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and largely regulatory rather than market-rate driven — a hard ~24% APR cap directly constrains the fees Qfin and funding partners can extract from any loan, independent of PBOC benchmark rates
key_input_costs: Cost of funds from bank/trust partners
Customer acquisition/marketing spend (now restricted by new rules)
Credit loss provisions on the capital-heavy book

recent_developments.event: Q2 2026 results: net revenue fell to $3.57bn equivalent (RMB terms), down ~32% YoY and down from $3.91bn in Q1 2026; non-GAAP net income fell to RMB454.9m from RMB945.9m in Q1 2026 and RMB1.85bn a year earlier (~76% YoY decline); loan facilitation/origination volume ~RMB63.4bn, down 2.5% sequentially; semi-annual dividend declared at US$46/ADS (~30% payout ratio) despite the earnings collapse

Management guided Q3 2026 non-GAAP net income to RMB400-500m, a 67-73% YoY decline, citing extremely tight funding supply, liquidity stress among market players, and new regulatory policies; guided to a further meaningful sequential decline in loan volume as risk controls tighten

Deutsche Bank downgraded QFIN to Hold from Buy, cutting its HK-listed price target to HK$50.70 from HK$93.20, citing the June 2026 liquidity crisis at peer Juzi Digitech that triggered a broad funding-partner pullback across the sector, and expectations that loan-book contraction extends into Q4 2026

Liquidity crisis at loan-facilitation peer Juzi Digitech triggered a sector-wide tightening of funding from banks and trust partners, directly constraining origination capacity at Qfin and other platforms

BofA Securities downgraded QFIN to Neutral from Buy, slashing its price target to $13.80 from $42.58 and cutting 2026-27 EPS estimates by 57% and 55% respectively, citing prolonged regulatory headwinds and the absence of share buybacks removing a near-term re-rating catalyst

China's Ministry of Public Security and National Financial Regulatory Administration launched a joint crackdown on illegal financial intermediaries ('black and gray market' loan brokers); separately, new rules from the PBOC and seven other ministries took effect restricting online marketing of loans/insurance/deposits by loan-assisting platforms, directly targeting the customer-acquisition channel

Company changed its English name from Qifu Technology, Inc. to Qfin Holdings, Inc. at its annual general meeting; stock tickers (QFIN on Nasdaq, 3660.HK on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange) were unchanged
Q1 2026 revenue declined 4.5% QoQ and 16.7% YoY, the first clear sign of the regulatory/funding-driven slowdown that intensified through Q2-Q3 2026

items.notes: Implies a 67-73% YoY decline from RMB1.85bn in Q3 2025; down sharply from RMB945.9m in Q1 2026 and RMB454.9m in Q2 2026, reflecting extremely tight funding supply, liquidity stress among market participants, and new regulatory policy implementation
Company is deliberately tightening risk controls and reducing volume in response to the challenging funding and regulatory environment, prioritizing asset quality over growth
US$46/ADS declared for H1 2026 despite the earnings decline; payout ratio policy held steady even as the earnings base shrank materially

guidance.management_commentary: Management attributed the sharp guidance cut to a sector-wide liquidity shock (triggered by peer Juzi Digitech's June 2026 crisis) that caused funding partners to pull back broadly, compounded by multiple new regulatory policies (rate caps, marketing restrictions, bank-partnership scrutiny) adding operational uncertainty. The company emphasized continued improvement in credit risk metrics (C-M2 delinquency ratio down 17% sequentially to 0.66%, 30-day collection rate up to 88.1%) as evidence of underwriting discipline even as it deliberately shrinks origination volume to preserve asset quality through the downturn.

bull_case: Despite the earnings collapse, Qfin's credit risk metrics (C-M2 delinquency, collection rates) are improving, suggesting the AI underwriting engine is working and the company is managing the downturn better than some peers
Regulatory-driven consolidation may ultimately benefit surviving scaled platforms like Qfin as smaller, less compliant competitors and brokers are forced out of the market

Valuation has been repriced sharply lower (BofA price target cut from $42.58 to $13.80) and already reflects much of the bad news, potentially offering asymmetric upside if the funding/regulatory environment stabilizes faster than feared
Company has continued paying a dividend (~30% payout ratio, US$46/ADS for H1 2026) even through the downturn, signaling some confidence in a baseline level of ongoing cash generation
Hong Kong dual listing (3660.HK) provides a fungible alternative trading venue that partially mitigates US delisting/HFCAA tail risk for holders of economic exposure to the business
bear_case: Earnings visibility has collapsed: non-GAAP net income guided down 67-73% YoY for Q3 2026, following a roughly 77% YoY decline already reported in Q2 2026 — this is a fundamentally impaired near-term earnings trajectory, not a temporary blip

Regulatory environment is actively hostile and escalating: rate caps, marketing restrictions, bank-partnership curbs, and a public-security-led crackdown on loan brokers are all compounding simultaneously in 2026, with no clear end date

Sector-wide funding/liquidity contagion (the Juzi Digitech crisis) shows the whole loan-facilitation industry's funding model is fragile and can seize up quickly, and management itself does not expect recovery before Q4 2026 at the earliest

Absence of share buybacks removes a key capital-return catalyst that supported the stock historically, per BofA's downgrade rationale, leaving dividends as the only capital return and vulnerable to further cuts if earnings stay depressed

100% China revenue concentration with underlying HFCAA/geopolitical delisting tail risk and RMB currency exposure offers US investors no diversification away from a single, heavily regulated, cyclically stressed market
